data: The J-mission suit (Apollo 15, 16, 17) — added a waist convolution that let astronauts sit in the Lunar Roving Vehicle

A7L derivative for the extended J-class lunar missions. The signature change was a waist-joint convolution that allowed astronauts to bend forward and sit in the Lunar Roving Vehicle — without it, the J-mission EVAs of Apollo 15, 16, and 17 would not have been possible. Same PLSS, OPS, and 3.7 psi pressure as A7L; same gold visor.
The J-mission suit — added a waist joint so astronauts could sit in the Lunar Rover

Sometimes a whole era of exploration turns on one joint. The A7LB was the A7L with a flexible convolution added at the waist — a small-sounding change that let an astronaut bend at the middle and sit down. That is the difference between walking a couple of kilometres from the lander and driving a rover across tens of them; between a two-hour moonwalk and a three-day field campaign. The last three Apollo landings — the long-stay science missions with the rover and, finally, a trained geologist — were only possible because the suit at last let people sit, reach, and work for hours at a stretch. The engineering headline is a waist joint; the result was the most productive science of the entire program.

A7L derivative for the extended J-class lunar missions. The signature change was a waist-joint convolution that allowed astronauts to bend forward and sit in the Lunar Roving Vehicle — without it, the J-mission EVAs of Apollo 15, 16, and 17 would not have been possible.
